This page reports the performance of Whittaker's core operations on a single machine. All timings
are wall-clock medians over three runs (one run for the largest sizes and MCMC). The benchmarks
establish a baseline for the current pure-Python/NumPy/SciPy implementation before any future
Rust or JAX acceleration work.

## Environment

```{python}
#| echo: false
import platform
import sys

import numpy as np
import scipy

import whittaker as wk

env_rows = [
    ("Whittaker", wk.__version__),
    ("Python", platform.python_version()),
    ("NumPy", np.__version__),
    ("SciPy", scipy.__version__),
    ("OS", f"{platform.system()} {platform.machine()}"),
    ("CPU", platform.processor() or "unknown"),
    ("CPU count", str(__import__("os").cpu_count())),
]

header = "| Component | Version |\n|---|---|"
rows = "\n".join(f"| {k} | {v} |" for k, v in env_rows)

from IPython.display import Markdown

Markdown(f"{header}\n{rows}")
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
import time
import altair as alt
import gc


def bench(fn, repeats=3):
    """Run `fn` `repeats` times and return the median wall-clock time in seconds."""
    times = []
    for _ in range(repeats):
        gc.collect()
        start = time.perf_counter()
        fn()
        times.append(time.perf_counter() - start)
    return float(np.median(times))


rng = np.random.default_rng(23)
```

## Sample size scaling

The most fundamental performance question is how fit time grows with the number of observations.
This benchmark fits a Gaussian GAM with a single cubic regression spline (`y ~ s(x, bs='cr')`)
using REML across a range of sample sizes. Cubic regression splines use a banded basis matrix, so
timing reflects the general P-IRLS cost without the $O(n^2)$ distance-matrix overhead of TPRS.

```{python}
#| echo: false
from whittaker.families.gaussian import Gaussian

sample_sizes = [500, 1_000, 2_000, 5_000, 10_000]
scaling_results = []

for n in sample_sizes:
    x = rng.uniform(0, 2 * np.pi, n)
    y = np.sin(x) + rng.normal(0, 0.3, n)
    data = {"x": x, "y": y}

    t = bench(lambda d=data: wk.GAM("y ~ s(x, bs='cr')").fit(d, method="REML"))
    scaling_results.append({"n": n, "seconds": round(t, 4)})
    del x, y, data
    gc.collect()

alt.Chart({"values": scaling_results}).mark_line(
    color="steelblue", strokeWidth=2, point=alt.OverlayMarkDef(size=50, filled=True),
).encode(
    x=alt.X("n:Q", scale=alt.Scale(type="log"), title="Sample size (n)"),
    y=alt.Y("seconds:Q", title="Fit time (seconds)"),
).properties(width=500, height=300, title="GAM fit time vs. sample size (Gaussian CRS, REML)")
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
header = "| n | Fit time (s) |\n|---:|---:|"
rows = "\n".join(f"| {r['n']:,} | {r['seconds']:.4f} |" for r in scaling_results)
Markdown(f"{header}\n{rows}")
```

Fit time grows roughly as $O(n \cdot k^2)$ where $k$ is the basis dimension (default 10). The
dominant cost is the Cholesky factorization of the penalized normal equations at each P-IRLS step.

## Smooth type comparison

Different smooth bases have different construction and penalty costs. This benchmark fixes $n =
3{,}000$ and compares the main smooth types on a Gaussian response with REML.

```{python}
#| echo: false
n_smooth = 3_000
x = rng.uniform(0, 2 * np.pi, n_smooth)
x2 = rng.uniform(0, 2 * np.pi, n_smooth)
y_smooth = np.sin(x) + rng.normal(0, 0.3, n_smooth)
data_smooth = {"x": x, "x2": x2, "y": y_smooth}

smooth_configs = [
    ("TPRS", "y ~ s(x)"),
    ("Cubic RS", "y ~ s(x, bs='cr')"),
    ("P-spline", "y ~ s(x, bs='ps')"),
    ("Cyclic CRS", "y ~ s(x, bs='cc')"),
    ("Tensor (te)", "y ~ te(x, x2)"),
]

smooth_results = []
for label, formula in smooth_configs:
    t = bench(lambda f=formula: wk.GAM(f).fit(data_smooth, method="REML"))
    smooth_results.append({"smooth": label, "seconds": round(t, 4)})

alt.Chart({"values": smooth_results}).mark_bar(color="steelblue").encode(
    x=alt.X("seconds:Q", scale=alt.Scale(type="log"), title="Fit time (seconds, log scale)"),
    y=alt.Y("smooth:N", title=None, sort=[r["smooth"] for r in smooth_results]),
).properties(width=500, height=200, title="Fit time by smooth type (n=3,000, Gaussian, REML)")
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
header = "| Smooth | Fit time (s) |\n|---|---:|"
rows = "\n".join(f"| {r['smooth']} | {r['seconds']:.4f} |" for r in smooth_results)
Markdown(f"{header}\n{rows}")
```

Cubic regression splines, P-splines, and cyclic splines are the fastest because they use banded
basis matrices. TPRS requires an $O(n^2)$ eigendecomposition of the distance matrix, making it
substantially slower at this sample size. Tensor products are the most expensive because they
construct a Kronecker product penalty over two marginal bases.

## Family comparison

Non-Gaussian families require iterative fitting (P-IRLS) with multiple Newton steps, so they are
inherently more expensive than the Gaussian case. This benchmark fixes $n = 3{,}000$ with a cubic
regression spline and compares across response distributions.

```{python}
#| echo: false
from whittaker.families.binomial import Binomial
from whittaker.families.gamma import Gamma
from whittaker.families.negative_binomial import NegativeBinomial
from whittaker.families.poisson import Poisson

n_fam = 3_000
x_fam = rng.uniform(0, 2 * np.pi, n_fam)
eta = 1.5 * np.sin(x_fam)

family_configs = [
    ("Gaussian", Gaussian(), eta + rng.normal(0, 0.3, n_fam)),
    ("Poisson", Poisson(), rng.poisson(np.exp(eta)).astype(float)),
    ("Binomial", Binomial(), rng.binomial(1, 1 / (1 + np.exp(-eta))).astype(float)),
    ("Gamma", Gamma(), rng.gamma(shape=2.0, scale=np.exp(eta) / 2.0)),
    ("Neg. Binomial", NegativeBinomial(), rng.negative_binomial(
        n=5, p=5 / (5 + np.exp(eta)),
    ).astype(float)),
]

family_results = []
for label, family, y_fam in family_configs:
    data_fam = {"x": x_fam, "y": y_fam}
    t = bench(lambda fam=family: wk.GAM("y ~ s(x, bs='cr')", family=fam).fit(data_fam, method="REML"))
    family_results.append({"family": label, "seconds": round(t, 4)})

alt.Chart({"values": family_results}).mark_bar(color="steelblue").encode(
    x=alt.X("seconds:Q", title="Fit time (seconds)"),
    y=alt.Y("family:N", title=None, sort=[r["family"] for r in family_results]),
).properties(width=500, height=200, title="Fit time by response family (n=3,000, CRS, REML)")
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
header = "| Family | Fit time (s) |\n|---|---:|"
rows = "\n".join(f"| {r['family']} | {r['seconds']:.4f} |" for r in family_results)
Markdown(f"{header}\n{rows}")
```

Gaussian fitting converges in a single P-IRLS step (it is a direct solve). Non-Gaussian families
typically require 3--8 iterations, with the Negative Binomial being the most expensive due to its
additional scale parameter estimation.

## Fitting method comparison

Whittaker supports several smoothness selection and inference methods. This benchmark compares
them on a Poisson GAM with a cubic regression spline at $n = 2{,}000$ to show the relative cost of
each approach.

```{python}
#| echo: false
n_method = 2_000
x_method = rng.uniform(0, 2 * np.pi, n_method)
y_method = rng.poisson(np.exp(1.5 * np.sin(x_method))).astype(float)
data_method = {"x": x_method, "y": y_method}

method_results = []

# Frequentist methods
for method in ["REML", "GCV", "ML"]:
    t = bench(lambda m=method: wk.GAM("y ~ s(x, bs='cr')", family=Poisson()).fit(data_method, method=m))
    method_results.append({"method": method, "seconds": round(t, 4)})

# VI
t = bench(lambda: wk.GAM("y ~ s(x, bs='cr')", family=Poisson()).fit(data_method, method="VI"))
method_results.append({"method": "VI", "seconds": round(t, 4)})

# MCMC (single run — expensive)
t = bench(
    lambda: wk.GAM("y ~ s(x, bs='cr')", family=Poisson()).fit(
        data_method, method="MCMC", mcmc_options={"n_samples": 200, "n_warmup": 100},
    ),
    repeats=1,
)
method_results.append({"method": "MCMC", "seconds": round(t, 4)})

method_order = [r["method"] for r in method_results]

alt.Chart({"values": method_results}).mark_bar(color="steelblue").encode(
    x=alt.X("seconds:Q", title="Fit time (seconds)"),
    y=alt.Y("method:N", title=None, sort=method_order),
).properties(
    width=500,
    height=200,
    title="Fit time by method (Poisson GAM, n=2,000, CRS)",
)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
header = "| Method | Fit time (s) |\n|---|---:|"
rows = "\n".join(f"| {r['method']} | {r['seconds']:.4f} |" for r in method_results)
Markdown(f"{header}\n{rows}")
```

REML, GCV, and ML have similar costs because they all use P-IRLS with outer smoothness selection.
VI adds optimization of the variational parameters on top of the P-IRLS initialization. MCMC is
the most expensive because it runs hundreds of leapfrog steps per sample, but it provides exact
posterior inference.

## Prediction throughput

Once a model is fitted, prediction speed matters for serving. This benchmark fits a single
Gaussian GAM on $n = 5{,}000$ observations and then times `predict()` across a range of
prediction-set sizes.

```{python}
#| echo: false
n_pred = 3_000
x_pred = rng.uniform(0, 2 * np.pi, n_pred)
y_pred = np.sin(x_pred) + rng.normal(0, 0.3, n_pred)
model_pred = wk.GAM("y ~ s(x, bs='cr')").fit({"x": x_pred, "y": y_pred}, method="REML")

pred_sizes = [100, 500, 1_000, 5_000, 10_000]
pred_results = []

for n_new in pred_sizes:
    x_new = rng.uniform(0, 2 * np.pi, n_new)
    new_data = {"x": x_new}
    t = bench(lambda d=new_data: model_pred.predict(d))
    pred_results.append({"n_new": n_new, "ms": round(t * 1000, 2)})

alt.Chart({"values": pred_results}).mark_line(
    color="steelblue", strokeWidth=2, point=alt.OverlayMarkDef(size=50, filled=True),
).encode(
    x=alt.X("n_new:Q", scale=alt.Scale(type="log"), title="Prediction set size"),
    y=alt.Y("ms:Q", title="Predict time (ms)"),
).properties(width=500, height=300, title="Prediction throughput")
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
header = "| n_new | Predict time (ms) |\n|---:|---:|"
rows = "\n".join(f"| {r['n_new']:,} | {r['ms']:.2f} |" for r in pred_results)
Markdown(f"{header}\n{rows}")
```

Prediction is dominated by design matrix construction (evaluating the basis functions at the new
covariate values) and a single matrix--vector multiply. It scales linearly with the prediction set
size.

## BigGAM vs. GAM scaling

`BigGAM` uses discretised covariates and compressed sufficient statistics to avoid building the
full $n \times p$ design matrix. This makes it slower than `GAM` at small sample sizes (due to
discretization overhead) but faster at large ones.

```{python}
#| echo: false
big_sizes = [1_000, 2_000, 5_000, 10_000, 25_000]
big_results = []

for n_big in big_sizes:
    x_big = rng.uniform(0, 2 * np.pi, n_big)
    y_big = np.sin(x_big) + rng.normal(0, 0.3, n_big)
    data_big = {"x": x_big, "y": y_big}

    reps = 1 if n_big >= 25_000 else 3

    t_gam = bench(
        lambda d=data_big: wk.GAM("y ~ s(x, bs='cr')").fit(d, method="REML"),
        repeats=reps,
    )
    big_results.append({"n": n_big, "seconds": round(t_gam, 4), "method": "GAM"})

    t_big = bench(
        lambda d=data_big: wk.BigGAM("y ~ s(x, bs='cr')", n_discrete=200).fit(d, method="fREML"),
        repeats=reps,
    )
    big_results.append({"n": n_big, "seconds": round(t_big, 4), "method": "BigGAM"})

    del x_big, y_big, data_big

alt.Chart({"values": big_results}).mark_line(
    strokeWidth=2, point=alt.OverlayMarkDef(size=50, filled=True),
).encode(
    x=alt.X("n:Q", scale=alt.Scale(type="log"), title="Sample size (n)"),
    y=alt.Y("seconds:Q", title="Fit time (seconds)"),
    color=alt.Color("method:N", title="Backend"),
    strokeDash=alt.StrokeDash("method:N"),
).properties(width=500, height=300, title="GAM vs. BigGAM fit time scaling")
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
# Pivot into a comparison table
gam_times = {r["n"]: r["seconds"] for r in big_results if r["method"] == "GAM"}
big_times = {r["n"]: r["seconds"] for r in big_results if r["method"] == "BigGAM"}

header = "| n | GAM (s) | BigGAM (s) | Faster |\n|---:|---:|---:|---|"
rows_list = []
for n_big in big_sizes:
    g = gam_times[n_big]
    b = big_times[n_big]
    faster = "BigGAM" if b < g else "GAM"
    rows_list.append(f"| {n_big:,} | {g:.4f} | {b:.4f} | {faster} |")
Markdown(f"{header}\n" + "\n".join(rows_list))
```

`BigGAM`'s discretized design matrix trades a small fixed overhead for dramatically better scaling.
At small sample sizes the overhead may make `BigGAM` slightly slower than `GAM`, but it quickly
becomes the faster option as $n$ grows and dominates for large-scale fitting.
